items.text: The first film in history, "La Sortie de l'Usine Lumière à Lyon," lasts just 46 seconds and was shot in 1895 in Lyon.
Al Pacino and Robert De Niro both appeared in "The Godfather Part II" without ever sharing a scene together.
The "Star Wars" theme composed by John Williams has become one of the most recognizable soundtracks in the world.
The series "Friends" was originally titled "Insomnia Cafe" before being renamed during development.
Three-strip Technicolor debuted in 1935 with "Becky Sharp," revolutionizing color cinema.
Sean Connery wore a toupee in every James Bond film because he had started losing his hair at age 21.
"Toy Story" in 1995 was the first feature film made entirely with computer-generated imagery.
Viggo Mortensen broke two toes kicking a helmet in "The Two Towers." His scream in the film is genuine.
HBO rejected the original "Game of Thrones" pilot because test audiences found it nearly incomprehensible.
Alfred Hitchcock never won the Academy Award for Best Director, despite five nominations.
The T-Rex roar in "Jurassic Park" is a mix of elephant, alligator, and tiger cub sounds.
Will Smith turned down the role of Neo in "The Matrix" to star in "Wild Wild West."
"The Office" theme song was recorded by The Scrantones, a band created specifically for the show.
The first sound film in history was "The Jazz Singer" in 1927, starring Al Jolson.
In "Titanic," the starry sky in the sinking scene was astronomically inaccurate. Cameron corrected it for the 3D re-release.
Bryan Cranston took the "Breaking Bad" role after it had been offered to John Cusack and Matthew Broderick.
The famous shower scene in "Psycho" required 7 days of filming for just 45 seconds of footage.
Ennio Morricone composed over 500 soundtracks in a career spanning more than sixty years.
The bullet time effect in "The Matrix" was achieved with 120 cameras arranged in a circle, firing in sequence.
"The Simpsons" is the longest-running primetime animated series in American television history.
Stanley Kubrick made Shelley Duvall repeat the baseball bat scene in "The Shining" 127 times.
The famous Wilhelm scream is a sound effect recorded in 1951 and used in over 400 films.
The first public television broadcast took place in London in 1936 via the BBC.
Heath Ledger isolated himself in a hotel room for weeks to build his Joker character in "The Dark Knight."
Hans Zimmer composed the "Inception" theme by slowing down Edith Piaf's "Non, je ne regrette rien."
The production of "Mad Max: Fury Road" took roughly fifteen years overall between development and filming.
Andy Serkis's motion capture performance as Gollum in "The Lord of the Rings" redefined the technique in cinema.
"Stranger Things" was rejected by over 15 networks before being picked up by Netflix.
Charlie Chaplin once entered a look-alike contest of himself and didn't win.
The cornfield in "Interstellar" was actually planted by the production and sold after harvest.
The first Academy Awards ceremony in 1929 lasted only 15 minutes, and winners had been announced months earlier.
Pedro Pascal was cast as the lead in "The Last of Us" after the series had already been in development for years.
The lightsaber sound in "Star Wars" was created by combining the hum of a film projector and an old television set.
Meryl Streep holds the record for most Oscar nominations as an actress, with twenty-one total nods.
The "Pulp Fiction" soundtrack contains no originally composed music — it's made entirely of pre-existing songs.
"Squid Game" became the most-watched non-English-language series in Netflix history.
Jim Carrey stayed in character as Andy Kaufman throughout the entire filming of "Man on the Moon."
The IMAX format was first introduced at Expo '70 in Osaka with a multi-screen film.
Robert Downey Jr. was considered an uninsurable risk before being cast as Iron Man in 2008.
HBO's "Chernobyl" was filmed almost entirely in Lithuania, at a real former Soviet nuclear power plant.
The piano in the theme of "The Pianist" was actually played by Adrien Brody, who trained for months.
Quentin Tarantino worked at a video rental store before becoming a director — that's where he built his film knowledge.
The first animated feature film in history was "El Apóstol" from 1917, an Argentine film now lost.
In "Inception," the spinning top at the end isn't Cobb's real totem — his original totem is his wedding ring.
"The Bear" required its actors to attend real professional cooking courses before filming began.
The THX Deep Note, the sound heard before many films in theaters, was generated in 1983 by a computer program.
Chadwick Boseman filmed several Marvel movies while privately battling colon cancer.
The iconic whistle in Sergio Leone's westerns was performed by Alessandro Alessandroni, a collaborator of Morricone.
"Parasite" by Bong Joon-ho was the first non-English-language film to win the Academy Award for Best Picture.
The snow in "Game of Thrones" was often chemically treated recycled paper made to look realistic.
Tom Hanks wasn't paid a fixed fee for "Forrest Gump": he chose a percentage of the gross, earning far more.
The velociraptor sounds in "Jurassic Park" were created by recording tortoises mating.
Keanu Reeves gave up a large portion of his "The Matrix" salary to increase the special effects budget.
David Lynch's "Twin Peaks" is considered the show that paved the way for modern prestige television.
The first film to gross over one billion dollars worldwide was James Cameron's "Titanic" in 1998.
Danny DeVito and Arnold Schwarzenegger became close friends on the set of "Twins" in 1988 and still are today.
Vangelis composed much of the "Blade Runner" score by improvising on a synthesizer while watching edited scenes.
"Money Heist" was originally conceived as a two-part miniseries for Spanish TV, before its global success on Netflix.
Dolby Atmos, introduced in 2012 with "Brave", places sounds at precise points throughout the cinema auditorium.
Toshiro Mifune turned down the roles of Obi-Wan Kenobi and Darth Vader offered to him by George Lucas for "Star Wars".
The Lumière brothers' first public screening took place on December 28, 1895, at the Grand Café in Paris.
Jenna Ortega improvised Wednesday's dance in the series "Wednesday", drawing inspiration from '80s goth scene movements.
The communicator opening sound in "Star Trek" was created using the noise of a lighter flipped open in reverse.
Morgan Freeman landed his first major film role at age 50, with "Street Smart" in 1987.
The soundtrack of Nicolas Winding Refn's "Drive" helped launch the synthwave genre into mainstream pop culture.
During the filming of "The Revenant", the crew endured temperatures as low as −25 °C in the Canadian wilderness.
"Fleabag" began as a one-woman stage show by Phoebe Waller-Bridge at the Edinburgh Festival in 2013.
The CinemaScope format was introduced in 1953 to compete with television by widening the cinema screen.
In "Fight Club", David Fincher placed a Starbucks cup in nearly every shot of the film.
Darth Vader's breathing sound was created by recording a scuba regulator placed inside a microphone.
Cate Blanchett won the Oscar for playing Katharine Hepburn in "The Aviator" — herself an Oscar winner.
The "Succession" theme composed by Nicholas Britell deliberately blends hip-hop and classical music.
"Shōgun" (2024) became the series with the most Emmy wins for a single season in television history.
Walt Disney holds the record for most Oscars won by a single person: he received twenty-two during his career.
Samuel L. Jackson has appeared in over 150 films, making him one of the most prolific actors in Hollywood.
Rain in movies often contains milk mixed with water to make it more visible on camera.
Christian Bale lost over 25 kg for "The Machinist" and regained 45 kg a few months later for "Batman Begins".
"Dark" was Netflix's first original German-language production, debuting in 2017.
The "Schindler's List" theme was performed on violin by Itzhak Perlman, personally chosen by Spielberg.
The first wireless TV remote, the 1956 Zenith Space Command, worked using mechanical ultrasonic signals.
Harrison Ford was a carpenter working at the studios when George Lucas noticed him for "Star Wars".
Large-scale digital de-aging of actors debuted in Scorsese's "The Irishman".
Natalie Portman trained for a year alongside a professional ballerina to prepare for "Black Swan".
"Mare of Easttown" starring Kate Winslet boosted tourism in the real Easttown Township in Pennsylvania.
Pink Floyd created "The Dark Side of the Moon" partly to score a film that was never made.
The first posthumous Oscar was awarded to Sidney Howard in 1940 for the screenplay of "Gone with the Wind".
Bill Murray agreed to "Ghostbusters" on the condition that Columbia would finance his film "The Razor's Edge".
The underwater scenes in "Avatar: The Way of Water" were filmed in a purpose-built 900,000-gallon tank.
Joaquin Phoenix lost over 23 kg for the role of Arthur Fleck in 2019's "Joker".
"Arcane" took six years of production before debuting on Netflix in 2021.
"The Godfather" theme was composed by Nino Rota, who had partially used it in a 1958 Italian film.
The Moviola, the first film editing device, was invented in 1924 and remained in use for decades.
Robin Williams improvised so much on set that his contracts included entire blank pages left free for him.
The LED Volume technology used in "The Mandalorian" projects 3D environments on massive screens behind the actors.
Christopher Nolan's "Oppenheimer" recreated the Trinity Test explosion without CGI, using only practical effects.
"Black Mirror" takes its title from the turned-off screens of phones and TVs, which reflect like dark mirrors.
Eminem's "Lose Yourself" from "8 Mile" was the first hip-hop song to win the Academy Award.
Kodachrome, the first color film for the general public, was introduced by Kodak in 1935.
Michael Keaton was cast as Batman in 1989 amid massive fan backlash, only to be acclaimed after the film's release.
"Ted Lasso" originated from an NBC promotional sketch to market the Premier League in the United States.
Steven Spielberg was rejected three times by the USC School of Cinematic Arts before becoming the most celebrated director of his generation.
In "Django Unchained", Leonardo DiCaprio actually cut his hand breaking a glass and continued acting through the scene.
The laugh tracks used in American sitcoms date back to the 1950s — some contain laughter from people who have since passed away.
"The Wire" was a ratings disappointment during its original run, but is now considered one of the greatest TV series ever made.
The grand piano used in "The Truman Show" theme was played by Burkhard Dallwitz, who co-composed the score with Philip Glass.
Michelle Yeoh won the Best Actress Oscar in 2023 for "Everything Everywhere All at Once", the first Asian woman in the category.
For "Cast Away", production halted for a full year to let Tom Hanks lose weight and grow out his beard.
The ARRI Alexa camera, introduced in 2010, became the most widely used digital cinema camera in Hollywood productions.
"Severance" on Apple TV+ transformed a former AT&T warehouse in New Jersey into the set for its Lumon Industries offices.
Hans Zimmer composed the "Interstellar" score without knowing the plot — Nolan only gave him a personal letter as guidance.
Anthony Hopkins was on screen for just 16 minutes in "The Silence of the Lambs", yet won the Oscar for Best Actor.
The first home video recorder, the Sony Betamax, hit the market in 1975, changing the way people watched TV.
To create WALL·E's voice, Ben Burtt processed his own voice through a vintage 1970s vocal synthesizer.
"Better Call Saul" was in development for two years before Vince Gilligan found the right tone to set it apart from "Breaking Bad".
The song "My Heart Will Go On" was included in "Titanic" against James Cameron's initial wishes.
Audrey Hepburn worked as a courier for the Dutch resistance during World War II, before becoming an actress.
"Tutto chiede salvezza" was one of the first Italian Netflix series based on a novel that won the Premio Strega Giovani.
The rotating hallway scene in "Inception" was built for real: a revolving cylindrical set thirty meters long.
Yorgos Lanthimos' "Poor Things" used fisheye lenses and hand-painted sets to create its surreal world.
The first sitcom in TV history was "Mary Kay and Johnny", broadcast by the DuMont Network in 1947.
Denzel Washington has won two Oscars: for "Glory" in 1990 and for "Training Day" in 2002.
Explosions in space as shown in movies are scientifically impossible — in a vacuum there is no air to carry shockwaves or sound.
"Succession" is loosely inspired by the Murdoch family dynamics, though creator Jesse Armstrong has never fully confirmed it.
Ryuichi Sakamoto composed the score for "The Last Emperor" and also acted in the film as a Japanese officer.
The 1922 "Nosferatu" was nearly destroyed: Bram Stoker's heirs won a court order to eliminate all copies of the film.
For "Alien", Ridley Scott didn't reveal the chestburster scene to the cast — the actors' horrified reactions are genuine.
The 4:3 aspect ratio dominated TV for decades. The shift to 16:9 only became standard with the arrival of high definition.
"Gomorrah - The Series" was sold in over 190 countries, becoming one of the most widely exported Italian TV productions.
The score for "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly" was recorded before filming — Leone directed scenes following the music.
Spike Lee financed his first film, "She's Gotta Have It" (1986), on a budget of just $175,000.
In "The Truman Show", Jim Carrey improvised the mirror line "Good morning, good afternoon, and good night."
Sandra Bullock and George Clooney in "Gravity" acted almost entirely inside a mechanical rig that simulated zero gravity.
"Peaky Blinders" takes its name from a real Birmingham gang active from the late 1800s to the early 1900s.
The Bee Gees' "Stayin' Alive" from "Saturday Night Fever" remains one of the best-selling singles in music history.
Greta Gerwig was the fifth woman in history to receive a Best Director Oscar nomination, for "Lady Bird".
Gary Oldman was nearly unrecognizable as Winston Churchill in "Darkest Hour" — the makeup took over three hours each day.
Green screen was first used in the 1940s, but only became dominant with the rise of digital cinema in the 2000s.
"Narcos" hired the brother of real DEA agent Steve Murphy as a consultant to ensure the series' historical accuracy.
Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross of Nine Inch Nails won the Oscar for the "The Social Network" score in 2011.
The first color film shot in Italy was "Totò a colori" in 1952, using Ferraniacolor, an Italian film stock.
For "Nope", Jordan Peele built an entire western town in the California desert as a permanent set.
Real-time ray tracing, now used in video games and virtual sets, simulates the actual physical behavior of light.
Netflix's "Baby Reindeer" is based on the real-life experience of its creator and star, Richard Gadd.
Angelo Badalamenti composed the "Twin Peaks" theme by improvising on piano while David Lynch described images to him aloud.
Buster Keaton performed all his stunts without a double, including the famous house facade falling on him in "Steamboat Bill, Jr."
Denis Villeneuve's "Dune" was filmed in Jordan, in the same deserts David Lean used for "Lawrence of Arabia".
The Steadicam was invented by Garrett Brown in 1975 and first used to iconic effect in "Rocky".
"Slow Horses" starring Gary Oldman is based on Mick Herron's novels, which were largely unknown until the Apple TV+ adaptation.
Wes Anderson always uses the same symmetrical color palette in his films — every frame is composed like a painting.
Federico Fellini coined the term "paparazzo" in his 1960 film "La Dolce Vita", inspired by a character in the movie.
Daniel Day-Lewis would retire from acting between films, working as a cobbler in Florence between "Gangs of New York" and "There Will Be Blood".
The line "Frankly, my dear, I don't give a damn" in "Gone with the Wind" was fined $5,000 for violating the Hays censorship code.
In "No Country for Old Men", Javier Bardem had to keep his iconic haircut for months off set because he couldn't cut it during production.
David Fincher's "Mindhunter" used facial prosthetics on actors to recreate the faces of real serial killers interviewed by the FBI.
The sinking ship effect in "Titanic" was achieved by tilting a 790-foot set built in Mexico.
Jack Nicholson improvised the line "Heeere's Johnny!" in "The Shining". Kubrick kept it even though it wasn't in the script.
"Squid Game" was written in 2008 by Hwang Dong-hyuk, but no one wanted to produce it for over ten years.
The first color TV broadcast in the United States took place in 1951 on CBS, but almost no one owned a compatible television set.
Florence Pugh landed her role in "Midsommar" with an audition where she cried so convincingly that Ari Aster cast her on the spot.
The lightsaber ignition sound in "Star Wars" was discovered by accident: Ben Burtt walked past a high-tension cable with his microphone.
Matteo Garrone's "Gomorrah" was filmed on location in Scampia with many non-professional actors who actually lived in the neighborhood.
The "Trainspotting" soundtrack helped make tracks like Underworld's "Born Slippy" famous well beyond the rave scene.
"The Great Beauty" won the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film in 2014, the first Italian film to do so since "Life Is Beautiful".
In "The Mandalorian", the physical Grogu puppet cost around $5 million and was operated by two puppeteers.
Timothée Chalamet learned to play piano for his role in "Call Me by Your Name", performing the pieces himself in the film.
"Boris" is considered one of the best Italian comedy series: it launched on a modest budget on Fox Italia in 2007.
The anamorphic Panavision format, introduced in the 1950s, is still favored by many directors today for its distinctive oval bokeh.
Guillermo del Toro built an entire museum of horror and film memorabilia in his home, called "Bleak House".
The "Stranger Things" theme was composed by Survive, a synthwave duo from Austin, in just a few weeks after a single meeting with the Duffers.
Alfonso Cuarón's "Roma" was the first Netflix film to receive a Best Picture nomination at the Oscars in 2019.
In "Apocalypse Now", Martin Sheen suffered a heart attack while filming in the Philippine jungle but returned to set a few weeks later.
Zendaya became the youngest lead actress to win an Emmy for "Euphoria" in the Outstanding Lead Actress in a Drama Series category.
"Parasite" was filmed on a set built entirely in a studio: the Kim family's house and the poor neighborhood don't exist in real life.
Sofia Coppola was the third woman in history nominated for the Best Director Oscar, for "Lost in Translation" in 2004.
For "The Batman", Robert Pattinson drew inspiration from Kurt Cobain to build his Bruce Wayne, with director Matt Reeves' approval.
The "Stranger Things" score is built on analog synthesizers from the '70s and '80s, notably the Roland Juno and the Sequential Prophet.
"True Detective" season one was filmed in Louisiana in chronological order, a rare choice for a modern TV production.
Miyazaki hand-draws most of the storyboards for Studio Ghibli films, even after turning eighty.
The 70mm film used in Tarantino's "The Hateful Eight" was projected with Ultra Panavision lenses, unused since the 1960s.
Sandra Oh was the first actress of Asian descent to receive a Lead Actress nomination at the Emmys.
In "Birdman", Alejandro González Iñárritu shot the film to appear as one continuous, unbroken take.
"Suburra" was the first Italian original series produced by Netflix, debuting in 2017.
The score for Spike Jonze's "Her" was composed by Arcade Fire and Owen Pallett, in a rare foray into film music.
A Foley artist recreates all ambient sounds for a film in a studio — footsteps, clothing, objects — using everyday materials.
Lady Gaga immersed herself in the character of Patrizia Reggiani for a year and a half during the production of "House of Gucci".
"The Lord of the Rings" was filmed entirely in New Zealand in a single continuous shoot lasting 438 days.
"Servant" on Apple TV+ was partly directed by M. Night Shyamalan, who filmed key episodes in his own home in Philadelphia.
The Academy Award has been nicknamed "Oscar" since 1939: the true origin of the name remains uncertain and debated to this day.
For her role in "Monster", Charlize Theron became unrecognizable with prosthetic makeup that took four hours every morning.
"1883" and "1923", spin-offs of "Yellowstone", were among the most expensive series ever produced for Paramount+.
Alexandre Desplat has scored eight films nominated for Best Picture at the Oscars, winning twice.
The CGI for Thanos's face in "Avengers: Endgame" used 150 facial markers on Josh Brolin's face during every scene.
Tilda Swinton is nearly unrecognizable in many of her roles: in 2018's "Suspiria" she played three different characters, including an elderly man.
Giuseppe Tornatore's "Cinema Paradiso" won the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film in 1990, launching the Sicilian director worldwide.
In "Mad Max: Fury Road", the Doof Warrior actually played a working flamethrower guitar mounted on the truck.
"Ripley" on Netflix was shot entirely in black and white along the Italian coast, in Atrani, Rome, and Venice.
Darth Vader's Imperial March didn't appear in the first "Star Wars": John Williams composed it only for "The Empire Strikes Back".
The first film with Dolby Stereo sound was "A Star Is Born" with Barbra Streisand in 1976, paving the way for multichannel audio.
Denis Villeneuve refused to use green screens for "Arrival": the alien shell was built as a physical set standing forty feet tall.
Marcello Mastroianni didn't speak English and learned his lines phonetically for his rare English-language films.
Matt Damon co-wrote the screenplay for "Good Will Hunting" with Ben Affleck on the backs of napkins during work breaks.
The role of Wolverine was offered to Russell Crowe, who turned it down and personally suggested Hugh Jackman's name.
"The Crown" rebuilt entire Buckingham Palace sets in a studio: no scenes were filmed in the actual royal palace.
Early nitrate film stock was extremely flammable: many silent films were lost in accidental fires.
John Travolta turned down the role of Forrest Gump before it was offered to Tom Hanks.
Laugh tracks in sitcoms are often mixed with real audience laughter to create a more natural effect.
The Coens' "Fargo" opens with "based on a true story," but it's entirely fictional — a deliberate narrative choice.
The first woman to win the Palme d'Or at Cannes as a director was Jane Campion in 1993 with "The Piano."
Edward Norton rewrote much of the "American History X" screenplay without director Tony Kaye's consent.
Netflix's "The Witcher" required hundreds of custom wigs, many made with real human hair sewn by hand.
VHS won the war against Betamax despite lower quality, thanks to longer tapes and lower costs.
Sandra Bullock returned the Razzie Award she'd won the day before receiving the Oscar for "The Blind Side" in 2010.
Akira Kurosawa deeply influenced George Lucas: "The Hidden Fortress" directly inspired the plot of "Star Wars."
HBO's "Chernobyl" was the first miniseries to surpass "Breaking Bad" as the highest-rated TV show on IMDb at the time of its debut.
Orange and blue dominate Hollywood posters because they are complementary colors that naturally attract the human eye.
Kate Winslet held her breath underwater for over seven minutes during the filming of "Avatar: The Way of Water."
Alberto Sordi started his career as a voice actor: he provided the Italian voice for Oliver Hardy of Laurel and Hardy.
Netflix's "Beef" was written by Lee Sung Jin based on a real road rage incident that happened to him on the highway.
The sound of the Millennium Falcon failing to start in "Star Wars" is the actual noise of a jammed 35mm projector.
Meryl Streep learned to play the violin for "Music of the Heart" with daily lessons for two months before filming.
The 1980 "Shōgun" was so popular in America that soy sauce sales rose significantly after it aired.
The first film shown on an airplane was in 1921, on an Aeromarine Airways flight aboard a seaplane.
In "Her," Scarlett Johansson replaced Samantha Morton as the voice of Samantha after the film had already been shot.
"The White Lotus" was filmed during the pandemic at the Four Seasons in Maui, with cast and crew quarantined at the hotel.
The first film to use surround sound was Disney's "Fantasia" in 1940, with the multi-speaker Fantasound system.
Woody Harrelson only learned as an adult that his biological father was a convicted hitman, an experience that shaped his role choices.
Sergio Leone shot very few takes per day but planned each one with obsessive precision before every scene.
Marvel's "Loki" introduced the multiverse concept that guided the entire Phase 4 and 5 of the MCU.
The letterbox format with black bars above and below the image was long hated by TV audiences in the '80s and '90s.
Adele initially refused to write the theme for "Skyfall" for James Bond, then changed her mind after reading the screenplay.
Kubrick made Tom Cruise repeat the walking scene in "Eyes Wide Shut" about 95 times before he was satisfied.
HBO's "My Brilliant Friend" was filmed in Caserta on a neighborhood set faithfully recreated from the 1950s.
The RED ONE digital camera in 2007 made digital cinema accessible to independent filmmakers at a previously unthinkable cost.
Jackie Chan performs his own stunts without a double and has fractured nearly every bone in his body throughout his career.
Vittorio De Sica's "Bicycle Thieves" (1948) is considered the masterpiece of Italian neorealism and was filmed with non-professional actors.
For "Anatomy of a Fall," Justine Triet wrote the dog's role specifically for Messi, a Border Collie who was already a seasoned actor.
"Yellowjackets" blends two timelines with different casts: the adult actresses didn't meet the younger ones until the première.
Digital color grading has almost entirely replaced chemical lab processing for defining a film's color palette.
Radiohead allowed the use of "Exit Music (For a Film)" in Baz Luhrmann's "Romeo + Juliet," one of the band's rare concessions.
Clint Eastwood almost always directs in one or two takes per scene: his fast style is legendary in the industry.
Hedy Lamarr, a 1940s Hollywood star, co-invented a frequency-hopping communication system that anticipated modern Wi-Fi.
For "Killers of the Flower Moon," Scorsese asked the Osage Nation to oversee every cultural detail of the film.
Apple TV+'s "Pachinko" was filmed in three languages — Korean, Japanese, and English — spanning four generations.
Dolby Vision HDR doubles the dynamic range of the image compared to the standard, approaching how the human eye perceives light.
Radiohead's Jonny Greenwood is also a film score composer: his work on "Phantom Thread" was nominated for an Oscar.
Christopher Lee read "The Lord of the Rings" every year and was the only cast member to have met Tolkien in person.
Paramount in Hollywood is the only major studio still physically located in the city of Los Angeles: all the others have moved.
In Celine Song's "Past Lives," the Seoul and New York scenes were shot with deliberately opposite color palettes.
Amazon Prime's "Fallout" recreated a post-apocalyptic Las Vegas on a set built in the Namibian desert.
The ratio 2.39:1 is the most common widescreen aspect ratio in modern blockbusters, also known as CinemaScope.
Al Pacino turned down the role of Han Solo in "Star Wars" because he found the script too confusing to understand.
The set of "Blade Runner 2049" included an e-waste dump built with tons of real garbage.
"The Bear" was filmed in a real Chicago restaurant kitchen: the actors took professional cooking classes before shooting.
Charlie Chaplin once entered a look-alike contest of himself and didn't win.
The first animated feature film in history was "El Apóstol", a 1917 Argentine film that is now lost.
The "Amélie" soundtrack by Yann Tiersen was partly composed before the film: Jeunet chose pre-existing pieces by the musician.
For "The Whale", Brendan Fraser wore a prosthetic suit weighing about 130 kg that required six hours to apply.
The first TV series broadcast in Italy was "The Adventures of Rin Tin Tin" in 1956, just months after RAI began transmitting.
Tony Gilroy's "Andor" was written as a novel before becoming a screenplay: each episode covers a self-contained narrative arc.
The sound of the Enterprise's sliding door in "Star Trek" was a paper bag dragged across a smooth floor.
Viggo Mortensen learned horse riding, swordfighting, and Elvish to play Aragorn in "The Lord of the Rings".
Ennio Morricone composed over 500 scores in his career, but didn't win his first competitive Oscar until 2016.
2024's "Shōgun" was filmed almost entirely in Japanese, a rare choice for an American production of that scale.
The term "blockbuster" comes from the queues that wrapped around the block: crowds literally "blocked" the streets.
The first film with synchronized dialogue was "The Jazz Singer" in 1927, marking the end of the silent film era.
Robert De Niro actually got a taxi driver's license and worked a few nights in New York to prepare for "Taxi Driver".
Apple TV+'s "Silo" built a ten-story vertical set to recreate the central spiral staircase of the underground bunker.
The T-Rex sound in "Jurassic Park" blends the calls of a baby elephant, an alligator, and a tiger cub.
Viola Davis is one of the few actresses to have won the so-called Triple Crown: an Oscar, an Emmy, and a Tony Award.
For "Ratatouille", the Pixar team took cooking classes at Michelin-starred Parisian restaurants for months.
"Skam" started as a Norwegian teen series in 2015 and was later adapted in over ten countries, including Italy.
The first permanent cinema was the Grand Café in Paris, but the first purpose-built venue was the Eden in La Ciotat in 1899.
The "Mission: Impossible" theme composed by Lalo Schifrin in 1966 is in 5/4 time, a rare meter in TV and film music.
Heath Ledger isolated himself in a hotel room for six weeks to craft the voice and mannerisms of the Joker in "The Dark Knight".
Rotoscoping, the technique of tracing live-action movement into animation, was patented in 1917 by Max Fleischer.
"Only Murders in the Building" was conceived after Steve Martin and Martin Short did a comedy tour together.
Hayao Miyazaki announced his retirement from filmmaking at least seven times over his career, returning to direct each time.
The first Oscar for Best Animated Feature was awarded in 2002: it went to DreamWorks' "Shrek".
John Williams has received over fifty Oscar nominations, more than any other living person.
For "Tár", Cate Blanchett learned to conduct a live orchestra and studied piano intensively for months.
The original pitch for "Lost" was developed in just eleven weeks by ABC, a record for a series of that complexity.
The iconic orange sky in "Mad Max: Fury Road" was achieved in post-production by boosting the saturation of the Namibian desert.
Sophia Loren won the Oscar in 1962 for "Two Women", the first actress to win for a non-English-language film.
The song "As Time Goes By" from "Casablanca" had been written in 1931, eleven years before the film.
Willem Dafoe has played both a hero (Jesus in "The Last Temptation of Christ") and the Green Goblin in "Spider-Man" in the same career.
Alfonso Cuarón's "Disclaimer" for Apple TV+ was shot on 35mm film, a rare choice for contemporary series.
For "Philadelphia", Tom Hanks lost 12 kg and visited hospital wards for months to prepare for the role.
"Inspector Montalbano" has been broadcast in over 65 countries, making it one of the most widely exported Italian series ever.
The world's first film festival was the Venice Film Festival, inaugurated in 1932.
Philip Glass composed the trilogy of scores for the documentaries "Koyaanisqatsi", "Powaqqatsi", and "Naqoyqatsi" over twenty years.
Ke Huy Quan returned to acting after a twenty-year break and won the Oscar with the very first film of his comeback.

The 1964 Tokyo Olympics were the first broadcast live worldwide via satellite and the first to feature instant replay on TV.
Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross won the Oscar for "The Social Network" in 2011, becoming the first rock musicians to win the award.
"Yellowjackets" was conceived by creators Ashley Lyle and Bart Nickerson during a road trip through the Canadian forests.
The first fully computer-generated film was Pixar's "Toy Story" in 1995. Production took four years and eight hundred thousand hours of rendering.
Bong Joon-ho keeps a notebook with over two hundred ideas for unmade films. Every few years he picks one and develops it.
For "Challengers", Luca Guadagnino filmed tennis scenes with cameras mounted on rackets and placed inside the balls.
The first woman to win the Golden Lion at Venice was Agnès Varda in 1985 with "Vagabond".
Netflix's "Ripley" used over thirty real locations in Italy, including Atrani, Naples, and Palermo, to recreate the 1960s atmosphere.
Hildur Guðnadóttir recorded the cello for the "Joker" soundtrack inside an abandoned power plant in Iceland.
For Alex Garland's "Civil War", urban battle scenes were filmed in Atlanta using genuinely abandoned buildings.
Michael Jordan refused to film "Space Jam" with actors in costumes. He insisted on traditional Looney Tunes animation.
The first use of green screen in cinema dates back to the 1930s. It was called "blue screen" because film stock was more sensitive to blue.
Pier Paolo Pasolini always cast non-professional actors in his lead roles, convinced that authenticity surpassed technique.
2024's "Shōgun" taught 16th-century Japanese to its modern actors with a team of linguists and historians specializing in the Sengoku period.
For "Sing Sing", Colman Domingo acted alongside real former inmates who played fictionalized versions of their own prison theater experiences.
The first sports documentary to win an Oscar was "When We Were Kings" in 1997, about the 1974 Ali-Foreman fight in Kinshasa.
Dario Marianelli composed the theme of "Atonement" by integrating the sound of a typewriter into the orchestra as a percussion instrument.
"Creature Commandos" is the first animated series from James Gunn's DC Studios universe. Each episode was storyboarded like a feature film.
The MPAA film rating system in the United States was introduced in 1968, replacing the Hays Code that had censored content since 1934.
For "Vermiglio", Maura Delpero filmed at 1,500 meters altitude in Trentino during winter, with temperatures dropping to minus twenty degrees Celsius.
Rain sounds in films are often amplified by pouring water onto metal sheets. Real rain is nearly inaudible to microphones.
2024's "Shōgun" had a full-scale 17th-century Dutch ship built in Vancouver's harbor for the scenes of Blackthorne's arrival.
Diego Maradona made a cameo in the 2008 film "L'allenatore nel pallone 2", his only cinematic appearance in an Italian movie.
Alberto Barbera has directed the Venice Film Festival since 2012. Under his leadership, the festival became the main launchpad for Oscar contenders.
For "Mad Max: Fury Road", George Miller filmed in the Namibian desert for over 120 days using more than 150 custom-built vehicles.
"Dark" was the first German series produced by Netflix. Its narrative structure across three timelines became a model for European serialized storytelling.
The first feature-length sound film was "The Jazz Singer" in 1927, with Al Jolson delivering the famous line "You ain't heard nothin' yet".
For "Joker", Joaquin Phoenix lost over 20 kg on a diet of boiled vegetables and one apple a day, preparing by studying archival footage of psychiatric patients.
The first direct broadcast satellite for television was Europe's OTS, launched in 1978 by ESA as a testbed for satellite TV transmissions.
Greta Gerwig became the first woman to direct a film that grossed over one billion dollars worldwide with "Barbie" in 2023.
"Narcos" blended real Colombian archival footage from the 1980s with scripted scenes to blur the line between documentary and fiction.
For "Gravity", Alfonso Cuarón developed an LED lighting system called the Light Box that projected space imagery onto the actors' faces in real time.
Robert De Niro got a real taxi license in New York and drove an actual cab at night to prepare for his role in Scorsese's "Taxi Driver".
"Stranger Things" was rejected by fifteen networks before Netflix picked it up. The Duffer Brothers were twenty-nine when they sold the project.
The first film to gross over $100 million in the US was Spielberg's "Jaws" in 1975, effectively inventing the concept of the summer blockbuster.
For "Her", Spike Jonze filmed in Shanghai, passing it off as a futuristic Los Angeles — the Chinese skyscrapers gave an advanced, unfamiliar city feel.
Clint Eastwood directs his films with very few retakes, often shooting just one or two takes per scene, believing the actor's first reaction is the most authentic.
HBO's "Chernobyl" recreated the reactor control room so accurately that nuclear engineers judged it nearly indistinguishable from the original.
Penélope Cruz was the first Spanish actress to win an Oscar, earning it in 2009 for Woody Allen's "Vicky Cristina Barcelona".
For "The Northman", Robert Eggers filmed the volcano scene in Iceland just a few kilometers from an active crater, with natural ash in the air.
Alexandre Desplat composed the "Grand Budapest Hotel" theme drawing on 1930s Central European chamber music, featuring balalaika and cimbalom.
"Severance" on Apple TV+ built fully furnished real offices with fictional documents — actors could open any drawer and find material consistent with the plot.
The first animated film ever made was Émile Cohl's "Fantasmagorie" in 1908. It lasted under two minutes and consisted of 700 hand-drawn frames.
For "Arrival", Denis Villeneuve had the alien ship interior built as a real vertical set. The actors walked on curved, tilted surfaces.
The T-Rex roar in "Jurassic Park" was created by combining a baby elephant's cry, an alligator's growl, and a tiger's roar.
The Coens' "Fargo" opens with the text "based on a true story" — it's actually entirely fictional, a deliberate narrative device by the directors.
"Money Heist" ("La casa de papel") initially flopped on Spain's Antena 3. Netflix relaunched it globally, turning it into an international phenomenon.
Kathryn Bigelow became the first woman to win the Best Director Oscar in 2010 for "The Hurt Locker", beating her ex-husband James Cameron.
For "Roma", Alfonso Cuarón rebuilt the entire street of his childhood in Mexico City, including shops and signs exactly as he remembered them.
Ludwig Göransson composed the "Black Panther" theme after traveling to Senegal to record local musicians playing traditional West African instruments.
The first home video recorder was the Sony Betamax, launched in 1975. It lost the format war to JVC's VHS despite offering superior quality.
"Derry Girls" became the most-watched series in Northern Irish television history, depicting the 1990s Troubles era with a comic, affectionate tone.
Al Pacino was nearly fired during the filming of "The Godfather" — Paramount executives found him too short and lacking the charisma needed for Michael.
For "Spencer", Kristen Stewart wore exact replicas of Princess Diana's outfits, tailored by the same fashion houses that had dressed the princess.
The first TV series broadcast in color was CBS's "The World Is Yours" in 1951, a short-lived educational program.
Sofia Coppola's "Priscilla" was filmed at the real Graceland in Memphis — one of the very few productions ever granted access to Elvis's estate.
Italian dubbing is considered among the world's best. Italy is one of the few countries where voice actors are celebrities recognized by the public.
Clint Mansell composed the haunting theme of "Requiem for a Dream" with the Kronos Quartet. The piece became one of the most used tracks in trailers.
"Pantheon" was one of the first adult animated series canceled and removed from its original platform, later saved by fans who distributed it online.
The first Cannes Film Festival was scheduled for 1939 but was canceled after the opening film's screening due to the outbreak of World War II.
For "Drive", Nicolas Winding Refn cast Ryan Gosling after the two sat in a car listening to '80s synth music together without speaking for an hour.
The first use of Steadicam in cinema was in "Rocky" in 1976. The run up the Philadelphia steps became iconic partly thanks to that fluid camera movement.
"Severance" used identical corridor sets mounted on wheels. The crew moved them around to create the illusion of an endless labyrinth on a low budget.
Viggo Mortensen learned to speak fluent Arabic for his role in "Captain Fantastic" and studies every language required by his characters.
Matteo Garrone's "Gomorrah" was filmed in the Vele di Scampia housing project with real residents, whom the director involved from the writing stage.
Michael Giacchino composed the melancholic theme of Pixar's "Up" in just a few hours. The dialogue-free opening sequence moves audiences with music alone.
Netflix's "Heartstopper" was adapted from a webcomic published for free on Tumblr and Tapas by Alice Oseman when she was nineteen years old.
The IMAX format was invented in Canada in 1970. The first IMAX film, "Tiger Child", was shown at the Osaka Expo on a 20-meter screen.
For "Anatomy of a Fall", Justine Triet had the actors improvise courtroom dialogue to capture spontaneous, believable reactions during the trial scenes.
Diane Keaton took her stage name from her mother. Her real surname is Hall — the same as the character she played in Woody Allen's "Annie Hall".
The first film soundtrack to sell over one million copies was "Saturday Night Fever" in 1977, driven by the Bee Gees.
"Only Murders in the Building" was created by Steve Martin, who wanted to make a comedy series about true crime podcasts after becoming an avid listener.
The first Olympics broadcast entirely in color on TV were the 1968 Mexico City Games, visible via satellite around the world.
For "Triangle of Sadness", Ruben Östlund filmed the storm scene on a real ship in the North Sea. Several actors genuinely suffered from seasickness.
Marcello Mastroianni never had a driver's license: on Fellini's sets he was driven everywhere by car, even for distances of just a few meters.
For "Parasite", Bong Joon-ho had the entire rich family's house built in a studio, including the garden with real grass and a working sprinkler system.
"Squid Game" was written in 2009 but rejected for ten years by every Korean studio: Netflix only picked it up in 2019.
Italy's first TV newscast aired on September 10, 1952 on RAI, hosted by Riccardo Paladini using only still images with commentary.
The bullet sounds in Matrix were made by plucking steel cables stretched between two poles and slowing the recording down by several octaves.
Ryuichi Sakamoto composed the theme for Bertolucci's "The Last Emperor", winning the Oscar in 1988: he was also an actor in the film.
Pelé turned down a cameo in 1981's "Escape to Victory" but then accepted a real role after reading the full screenplay.
For "The Zone of Interest", Jonathan Glazer placed ten hidden cameras in the house and let the actors perform with no visible crew.
"Gomorrah" the series was filmed in Naples with police escorts: some sets had to be relocated for safety reasons related to the Camorra.
The first color feature film shot in Italy was "Totò a colori" in 1952, using the Italian-made Ferraniacolor process.
The dolly, a cart on rails for smooth camera movements, was first used systematically by Murnau in "The Last Laugh" in 1924.
Max Richter composed "Sleep", an eight-hour album meant to be listened to while sleeping: his music appears in dozens of films and TV series.
Usain Bolt repeatedly turned down offers for a biopic about his life, saying no actor could run convincingly enough.
For "Io capitano", Matteo Garrone interviewed hundreds of real migrants to reconstruct the journey from Africa to Europe as faithfully as possible.
Tim Burton's "Wednesday" made Jenna Ortega a global star: the dance scene was choreographed by the actress herself, inspired by '80s goth dancing.
Anna Magnani won the Oscar in 1956 for "The Rose Tattoo": she received the news in Rome at four in the morning and went back to sleep.
The first film shot with a drone was an experimental short in 2012: today drones have replaced most helicopter aerial shots.
Vangelis composed the "Blade Runner" theme by improvising on Yamaha CS-80 synthesizers: he never wrote the score on paper.
The 2017 documentary "Icarus" started as a cycling doping experiment and ended up exposing Russia's state-run anti-doping fraud.
For "Dune", Denis Villeneuve banned the color green on set to maintain the desert aesthetic: even the catering food was chosen accordingly.
"Peaky Blinders" was created by Steven Knight based on stories from his father, who grew up in Birmingham's Small Heath neighborhood.
The first film released simultaneously in theaters and on streaming was "Trolls World Tour" in 2020, during the pandemic.
The CinemaScope format was introduced in 1953 with "The Robe": it used anamorphic lenses to project panoramic images on wide screens.
Philip Glass scored "Koyaanisqatsi" using only repetitive notes and choirs: the film has no dialogue or narration, just images and music.
Roger Federer produced a documentary about his career in 2024 using never-before-seen private footage, including childhood recordings from Basel.
For 2024's "Nosferatu", Robert Eggers had a castle built in the Czech Republic and artificially aged it for six months before filming.
Apple TV+'s "Silo" built a functional three-story vertical set for the spiral staircase: the actors actually climbed hundreds of steps.
The first honorary Oscar was awarded to Charlie Chaplin in 1929 during the very first Academy Awards ceremony.
For explosions in films, effects teams often use cornstarch and gasoline: the starch creates the cloud, the gasoline the orange flash.
Ennio Morricone and Sergio Leone met as children at an elementary school in Rome: neither remembered it when they started working together.
For "The Brutalist", Brady Corbet shot on VistaVision film, a 1950s format used to achieve a sharper image on panoramic screens.
Amazon's "Rings of Power" built massive sets in New Zealand but dismantled them after the first season, relocating production to the UK.
Vittorio De Sica found the young lead of "Bicycle Thieves" in a crowd of extras: Lamberto Maggiorani was a factory worker with no acting experience.
Rotoscoping, the technique of tracing movement from live-action footage frame by frame, was patented by the Fleischer brothers in 1917.
Wes Anderson always uses the same color palette in his films: every color is coded in a Pantone catalog he shares with the crew.
For "Flow", Latvian director Gints Zilbalodis animated most of the film alone in his apartment before securing funding to complete it.
"Ripley" was filmed in Atrani on the Amalfi Coast, chosen for its small size which allowed total control over every shot.
The first stereoscopic 3D film released in theaters was "Bwana Devil" in 1952: audiences wore glasses with red and green lenses.
Rain in films is lit from behind with strong lights: filmed from the front, it would be virtually invisible to the camera.
Tōru Takemitsu composed the score for Kurosawa's "Ran" inspired by Mahler: the two clashed over it, but the result was universally praised.
"The Last Dance" was only possible because Michael Jordan agreed in 2016 to release footage the NBA had filmed during the 1997-98 season.
For "Saltburn", Emerald Fennell rented a real 17th-century English aristocratic estate and furnished it with authentic period objects.
Netflix's "3 Body Problem" adapted Liu Cixin's Chinese novel: the creators of "Game of Thrones" developed it over four years.
Roberto Rossellini shot "Rome, Open City" in 1945 right after the war, with film stock bought on the black market and actors found on the street.
Blue screen was replaced by green screen in the '90s because green is farther from human skin tones and easier to isolate digitally.
A.R. Rahman composed the theme for "Slumdog Millionaire" blending tabla, synths, and Bollywood choirs: he won two Oscars the same night in 2009.
Serena Williams consulted on "King Richard" and insisted every tennis scene be technically accurate in both strokes and footwork.
For "La La Land", Damien Chazelle had Emma Stone and Ryan Gosling rehearse dancing for three months before filming: no doubles were used.
Marcello Mastroianni was nominated for the Oscar three times without ever winning: his last nomination came in 1988 for Nikita Mikhalkov's "Dark Eyes".
HBO's "The Penguin" was filmed in New York during winter: Colin Farrell spent four hours a day in prosthetic makeup to become Oz Cobb.
Akira Toriyama drew the entire Dragon Ball saga alone for eleven years, publishing 519 weekly chapters in Weekly Shōnen Jump from 1984 to 1995.
Hayao Miyazaki announced his retirement at least seven times throughout his career, only to return each time to direct a new film for Studio Ghibli.
Katsuhiro Otomo's "Akira" in 1988 used over 160,000 hand-drawn frames, a record for Japanese animation at the time.
Eiichiro Oda's One Piece is the best-selling manga in history, with over 500 million copies in circulation worldwide.
Hideaki Anno created Evangelion during a severe personal depression: Shinji Ikari's mental state directly reflects the director's own struggles.
Cristina D'Avena sang over 700 theme songs for anime and cartoons on Italian television, becoming the voice of childhood for entire generations.
Studio Ghibli was founded in 1985 by Miyazaki and Takahata using profits from "Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind", released before the studio existed.
Miyazaki's "Spirited Away" won the Golden Bear at Berlin in 2002 and the Oscar: it remains the only anime film to have won both awards.
Masashi Kishimoto drew Naruto for fifteen consecutive years with very few breaks, often sleeping at the Shūeisha studio to meet deadlines.
The 1996 finale of "Neon Genesis Evangelion" was made with almost no budget: the last two episodes used pencil sketches and still images.
Osamu Tezuka, creator of Astro Boy, is considered the father of modern manga. He introduced the large eyes inspired by 1940s Disney films.
"Dragon Ball Z" was dubbed into Italian with voices that became iconic: Paolo Torrisi voiced Goku for over a decade.
Studio MAPPA produced the final season of "Attack on Titan" after WIT Studio stepped down due to the complexity of the required animation.
Kentaro Miura worked on "Berserk" for over thirty years without completing it. After his passing in 2021, his assistants continued the manga.
Shin'ichirō Watanabe's "Cowboy Bebop" blended jazz, blues, and funk into animation. Yoko Kanno's soundtrack is considered one of the finest ever composed for a series.
The first episode of "Pokémon" aired in Japan on April 1, 1997. The series has surpassed 1,200 episodes, making it one of the longest-running anime.
Sailor Moon was one of the first shōjo manga to feature shōnen-style action scenes, influencing the magical warrior genre for decades to come.
"Death Note" was controversial in some countries: in China, replica notebooks were banned over concerns that students might imitate the concept.
Yoshihiro Togashi, author of "Hunter x Hunter", is known for long hiatuses between story arcs, caused by severe chronic back problems.
The 1995 "Ghost in the Shell" deeply influenced the Wachowskis: "The Matrix" draws several visual and thematic concepts from Mamoru Oshii's film.
Gō Nagai created Mazinger Z in 1972, inventing the mecha genre with pilot-operated robots. The Italian theme song remains beloved to this day.
Toei Animation, founded in 1948, is the studio behind Dragon Ball, One Piece, and Sailor Moon — the oldest Japanese animation studio still active.
"Demon Slayer: Mugen Train" in 2020 surpassed "Spirited Away" as the highest-grossing film in Japanese box office history.
Kyoto Animation is celebrated for its obsessive background detail: every scene is painted with realistic precision based on photographic location scouting.
Eiichiro Oda sleeps about three hours a night during One Piece serialization, working on chapters seven days a week since 1997.
Miyazaki's "Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind" inspired Japan's environmental movement in the 1980s with its message about coexistence with nature.
The Italian dub of "Lupin III" made the character more ironic and carefree than the original, turning it into a cult TV classic in 1980s Italy.
Akira Toriyama also designed the characters for the Dragon Quest and Chrono Trigger video games, bridging the manga and gaming worlds.
Mamoru Hosoda left Studio Ghibli after auditioning to direct "Howl's Moving Castle". He later founded his own Studio Chizu.
"Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood" held the top score on MyAnimeList for years, the world's largest anime database.
MAPPA's "Jujutsu Kaisen" became a global phenomenon in 2020: the manga went from modest print runs to millions of copies in just a few months.
Isao Takahata directed "Grave of the Fireflies" in 1988. The film is so emotionally intense that Studio Ghibli paired it with "Totoro" to balance the mood.
Rumiko Takahashi, creator of Urusei Yatsura, Ranma ½, and Inuyasha, is one of the most prolific and best-selling female mangaka in history.
The Italian theme song for "Saint Seiya" sung by Massimo Dorati became a hit: its rock rhythm made it unforgettable for an entire generation.
"Neon Genesis Evangelion" was re-dubbed in Italian for Netflix in 2019 with an entirely new cast, dividing fans between the old and new versions.
Studio Bones, founded by former Sunrise animators, is known for "My Hero Academia" and "Fullmetal Alchemist", favoring traditional animation over CGI.
Makoto Shinkai created his first short film "She and Her Cat" in 1999 almost entirely alone, from drawing to editing, in his apartment.
Makoto Shinkai's "Your Name" in 2016 broke every record for an anime film at the global box office, grossing over $250 million.
Hajime Isayama, creator of "Attack on Titan", worked at an internet café before his manga was accepted by Bessatsu Shōnen Magazine.
"Sakuga" — sequences animated at higher quality than the rest of an episode — has become a hallmark of modern Japanese animation.
Naoko Takeuchi, creator of Sailor Moon, holds a degree in chemistry. Each Sailor warrior is named after a planet in our solar system.
Katsuhiro Otomo spent eight years completing the "Akira" manga, publishing over two thousand pages in Young Magazine from 1982 to 1990.
Voice actress Masako Nozawa voices Goku, Gohan, and Goten in Japanese, lending her voice to three generations of the same family for nearly forty years.
"Grave of the Fireflies" is not technically a Studio Ghibli film: it was produced by Shinchōsha and only distributed alongside "Totoro" by the studio.
Satoshi Kon died at 46 in 2010, leaving "Dreaming Machine" unfinished. His four completed films influenced directors like Darren Aronofsky and Christopher Nolan.
"Dragon Ball" began as a retelling of the classic Chinese novel "Journey to the West": Goku is inspired by the monkey king Sun Wukong.
Studio Madhouse, founded in 1972, produced classics like "Trigun", "Death Note", and "One Punch Man", known for faithful manga adaptations.
Yoko Kanno composed the "Cowboy Bebop" soundtrack before many scenes were animated: Watanabe built episodes around the music.
"Evangelion: 3.0+1.0", the final Rebuild film, was released in 2021 after nine years of production. Hideaki Anno called it his definitive farewell to the series.
Tezuka produced "Astro Boy" as a TV series in 1963: it was the first anime broadcast on a weekly schedule, establishing the format still used today.
"Goldorak" arrived in Italy in 1978 and became the first anime to turn into a mass cultural phenomenon on Italian television.
Monkey Punch created Lupin III in 1967, inspired by Maurice Leblanc's thief Arsène Lupin, setting it in a modern, ironic world.
Yoshiyuki Tomino created Gundam in 1979, inventing the "real robot" genre: mecha had realistic technical limits and were no longer invincible.
"Slam Dunk" caused a basketball boom in 1990s Japan: school basketball club enrollments skyrocketed across the country.
Footballers like Zidane, Del Piero, and Fernando Torres cite "Captain Tsubasa" as a childhood inspiration that drove them to play.
"Detective Conan" has been serialized since 1994 with over 1,100 chapters: the protagonist, de-aged in chapter one, still hasn't returned to adulthood.
"One Punch Man" started as a rough webcomic by ONE: Yusuke Murata's professional redraw turned it into a worldwide cult manga.
Studio Trigger was founded in 2011 by Hiroyuki Imaishi and other ex-Gainax staff: their explosive, colorful style became a recognizable trademark.
Gainax was founded in 1984 by sci-fi fan college students: on a shoestring budget they produced "Evangelion", one of the most influential anime ever.
Tatsuki Fujimoto, creator of "Chainsaw Man", was 24 when serialization began: his unpredictable storytelling style divided readers.
CLAMP is a four-woman manga collective active since 1987: they created "Cardcaptor Sakura", "X", and "xxxHOLiC", spanning every genre.
Tokyo's Comiket is the world's largest self-published comics fair: held twice a year, each edition draws over half a million visitors.
Doraemon has been Japan's official cultural ambassador since 2008: the 22nd-century robot cat represents the country at diplomatic events.
"Fist of the North Star" drew from Bruce Lee for Kenshiro and "Mad Max" for its post-apocalyptic world: the manga debuted in 1983 on Shōnen Jump.
Tsukasa Hojo drew Shinjuku so precisely in "City Hunter" that fans used his manga as a guide to navigate the Tokyo district.
Tsugumi Ohba, writer of "Death Note" and "Bakuman.", has never revealed their identity: the name remains a mysterious pseudonym to this day.
Tite Kubo designed "Bleach" characters starting from fashion: each Shinigami had a full wardrobe planned but never fully shown.
"Vinland Saga" began as a Viking action manga and evolved into a story about non-violence: the thematic shift surprised readers and critics alike.
Weekly Shōnen Jump is the best-selling manga magazine in the world: it launched Dragon Ball, One Piece, Naruto, Bleach, and dozens of other legends.
Miyazaki rejects CGI as the basis of animation: Ghibli films are hand-drawn and hand-painted, a process that takes years for each work.
Ghibli Museum tickets in Mitaka sell out within minutes each month: Miyazaki insisted on a daily visitor cap to preserve its intimate atmosphere.
The bathhouse in "Spirited Away" was inspired by Dōgo Onsen in Matsuyama, a hot spring facility active for over a thousand years.
Totoro originated from a sketch Miyazaki drew in the 1970s: the character waited over a decade before becoming the beloved 1988 film.
"Princess Mononoke" required three years and 144,000 frames, 80,000 of which were digitally retouched: it was Ghibli's most expensive film at the time.
Satoshi Kon's "Paprika" came out in 2006: Christopher Nolan cited it as an inspiration for the dream sequences in "Inception" (2010).
Darren Aronofsky bought the rights to Satoshi Kon's "Perfect Blue" to recreate the bathtub scene in "Requiem for a Dream".
"Fruits Basket" got a full remake in 2019 because the 2001 series had altered the manga's ending, disappointing author Natsuki Takaya.
Tatsuya Endo's "Spy x Family" became one of the best-selling manga of 2022: its mix of espionage, telepathy, and family won over every audience.
Leiji Matsumoto, creator of Captain Harlock and Galaxy Express 999, defined the space aesthetic of Japanese animation for an entire generation.
"Sazae-san" holds the record for the longest-running anime: on air since 1969, it has surpassed 2,700 episodes on Japanese television.
In Italy, "Goldorak" drew higher ratings than the evening news: the late-1970s anime phenomenon revolutionized children's television in the country.
Megumi Hayashibara is one of Japan's most celebrated voice actresses: she voiced Rei Ayanami in Evangelion, Lina in Slayers, and Faye in Cowboy Bebop.
Japanese animators often work with low pay and extreme hours: the anime industry only recently began reforms to improve working conditions.
Mamoru Oshii set "Ghost in the Shell" in Hong Kong, not Tokyo: the city's architecture inspired cyberpunk more than modern Japan did.
Studio Ufotable revolutionized "Demon Slayer" with a blend of 2D animation and CGI: the fight scenes went viral on social media worldwide.
Tezuka's Astro Boy inspired generations of robotics engineers: Honda stated that the ASIMO robot was influenced by the little character's design.
"Crayon Shin-chan" is adult humor in Japan despite its five-year-old protagonist: in Italy it was broadcast as a children's anime.
Studio WIT animated the first three seasons of "Attack on Titan" with 3D maneuvering scenes that required new digital animation techniques.
The name "Naruto" comes from narutomaki, the spiral fish cake slice in ramen: the protagonist's favorite dish.
Studio Pierrot animated both "Naruto" and "Bleach", two of the shōnen "Big Three": the studio specializes in long-running action series.
Evangelion merchandise generates billions of yen yearly: in Japan, Eva-branded products range from razors to car insurance policies.
Ai Yazawa's "Nana" went on hiatus in 2009 due to the author's health issues and was never completed: fans have awaited an ending for over fifteen years.
Takehiko Inoue, creator of "Slam Dunk", also made "Vagabond" about Musashi Miyamoto, featuring watercolor-painted panels of museum-level quality.
Dr. Mashirito in "Dr. Slump" was modeled by Toriyama after his editor Kazuhiko Torishima: the manga villain bore his supervisor's face.
Mangaka serialized in weekly magazines produce about 19 pages per week: the pace is so intense that many work with teams of assistants.
"Heidi" (1974), directed by Takahata with layouts by Miyazaki, was a huge hit in Europe: many viewers didn't know it was a Japanese anime.
Rumiko Takahashi's "Ranma ½" featured a protagonist who changed sex upon contact with cold water: a novel idea blending martial arts and comedy.
"Lupin III" was among the first anime series aired in prime time in Italy: Roberto Del Giudice's dubbing became as iconic as the original.
Hosoda's "The Girl Who Leapt Through Time" (2006) was made on a modest budget but won numerous awards, relaunching the director's career.
Kōhei Horikoshi, creator of "My Hero Academia", drew inspiration from Spider-Man and Western superheroes to craft a shōnen manga with American comic flair.
Hirohiko Araki, creator of "JoJo's Bizarre Adventure", has been drawing since 1987 and looks so young that fans joke he's a vampire like Dio Brando.
Gunpla (Gundam plastic model) kits sell over 20 million units a year. Bandai built an 18-meter-tall Gundam statue in Yokohama.
"Sailor Moon" introduced reusable animated transformation (henshin) sequences: they saved budget and became a hallmark of the mahō shōjo genre.
Shinichirō Watanabe pitched "Cowboy Bebop" as a series about a jazz group. The sponsor insisted on adding gunfights and spaceships.
"Doraemon" has been translated into over 50 languages. In many Asian countries, the robot cat is more recognizable than Mickey Mouse.
Hirohiko Araki references rock music in every "JoJo" name: Dio, Zeppeli, Speedwagon, Jotaro Kujo, and the Stands all come from famous bands and songs.
Miyazaki personally drew every single frame of the train ride scene in "Spirited Away", refusing any assistance.
"Nadia: The Secret of Blue Water" was directed by Hideaki Anno before Evangelion. NHK intervened multiple times over the show's overly dark tone.
The Italian dub of "Dragon Ball" changed many technique names. Kamehameha was kept, but Onda Energetica became a uniquely Italian trademark.
"Saint Seiya" was far more successful in France, Italy, and Brazil than in Japan, where its ratings were modest.
Akemi Takada designed the characters for "Urusei Yatsura", "Creamy Mami", and "Kimagure Orange Road". Her style defined 1980s anime aesthetics.
"Mob Psycho 100" is ONE's second work after "One Punch Man". Studio Bones' animation turned his minimalist drawings into visually stunning scenes.
Kyoto Animation was struck by an arson attack in 2019 that killed 36 people. The studio recovered and resumed production with worldwide support.
Giorgio Vanni, after Cristina D'Avena, is Italy's most famous anime theme singer. "Pokémon" and "One Piece" are among his best-known songs.
"GTO - Great Teacher Onizuka" popularized school stories with an adult protagonist. Tōru Fujisawa's manga sold over 50 million copies.
Kunihiko Ikuhara left Toei after directing "Sailor Moon S" and created "Utena", a series that defied every narrative and visual convention of the genre.
"Lupin III: The Castle of Cagliostro" (1979) was Miyazaki's directorial debut. Spielberg called it one of the greatest adventure films ever made.
Togashi's "Yu Yu Hakusho" preceded "Hunter x Hunter". The series ended abruptly because the author was exhausted from weekly serialization.
Gō Nagai's "Devilman" (1972) was one of the first manga to feature a tragic, apocalyptic ending. It deeply influenced "Evangelion" and "Berserk".
Yoshiaki Kawajiri directed "Ninja Scroll" in 1993 on a limited budget. The film became a Western cult classic and paved the way for adult-oriented anime.
"Captain Tsubasa" was created by Yōichi Takahashi in 1981. The soccer field is intentionally exaggerated in scale to add more dynamism to the action.
Masakazu Katsura, creator of "Video Girl Ai" and "Zetman", is also the official illustrator for "Tiger & Bunny". His realistic style influenced many mangaka.
"Cells at Work!" turned the human body into a narrative world: red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets became characters fighting bacteria and viruses.
The OVA (Original Video Animation) format was born in 1983 with Mamoru Oshii's "Dallos": anime sold directly on home video, bypassing TV broadcast.
"Porco Rosso" is the only Ghibli film with an Italian protagonist. Miyazaki set the story in the 1920s Adriatic, inspired by his passion for aviation.
Tetsuo Hara, illustrator of "Fist of the North Star", produced top-quality pages at record speed. His assistants struggled to keep up with him.
"Serial Experiments Lain" (1998) anticipated themes like online identity and virtual life years before social networks existed.
"Akira" was produced with a record budget of 1.1 billion yen in 1988. Characters had lip movements synced to pre-recorded dialogue, a rarity for anime.
"Candy Candy" (1976) was a phenomenon in Italy but remains locked in a legal dispute between the writer and the artist. Reprints are impossible.
Japanese limited animation was pioneered by Tezuka to cut costs: it used 8–12 frames per second instead of Disney's standard 24.
"Made in Abyss" by Akihito Tsukushi started as a webcomic. Its dark story set in a seemingly childlike world surprised both audiences and critics.
Megumi Ogata, the Japanese voice of Shinji in Evangelion, is a woman. In Japan, it's tradition for teenage boys to be voiced by female actors.
"Mushishi" by Yuki Urushibara won the prestigious Kodansha Manga Award in 2006. The anime adaptation is considered one of the most contemplative ever made.
Eiichiro Oda has stated that One Piece is about 80% complete. The manga exceeds 110 volumes and has been serialized for over 27 years.
Watanabe's "Samurai Champloo" blended Edo-era samurai with modern hip-hop. The late Nujabes' soundtrack helped define a genre: lo-fi hip-hop.
Rumiko Takahashi is the best-selling female mangaka in history. Her combined works have sold over 200 million copies worldwide.
"Space Battleship Yamato" (1974) was the first anime to create organized fandom in Japan, with dedicated clubs, fanzines, and conventions.
Kana Hanazawa is one of the most sought-after voice actresses of the 2010s and 2020s, voicing characters in hundreds of anime from "Angel Beats!" to "Psycho-Pass".
"Banana Fish" by Akimi Yoshida ran from 1985 to 1994 in a shōjo magazine — despite being an action thriller set in New York, not a shōnen title.
Studio Sunrise, creator of Gundam, was renamed Bandai Namco Filmworks in 2022. The Sunrise brand remains as a label for anime productions.
"Planetes" by Makoto Yukimura depicted space debris collection in 2003. NASA later acknowledged the manga as surprisingly accurate on the subject.
Nobuo Uematsu, composer of Final Fantasy, was influenced by 1970s anime soundtracks. The line between video game and anime music has always been thin.
Studio Trigger's "Cyberpunk: Edgerunners" was the anime that revived sales of "Cyberpunk 2077" in 2022, reversing the game's negative perception.
"Ashita no Joe" (1970) sparked such empathy in Japan that fans held a real public funeral for a character who died in the series.
Yōji Enokido wrote episodes for "Sailor Moon", "Evangelion", and "FLCL". His surreal, psychological style is recognizable across all three series.
"Steins;Gate" is based on real time-travel theories by John Titor, a supposed time traveler who appeared on internet forums in 2000.
In Italy, anime theme songs were rewritten from scratch with original Italian lyrics. Almost none kept the Japanese melody or text.
Miyazaki's "The Boy and the Heron" was released in Japan in 2023 with no trailers or promotional campaign. Studio Ghibli only released a single poster.
Naoki Urasawa, creator of "Monster" and "20th Century Boys", is also a musician. He plays guitar in a band and has released original albums.
"Macross" (1982) combined mecha, pop music, and love triangles — an unprecedented formula that influenced the entire genre for the next forty years.
"Rurouni Kenshin" by Nobuhiro Watsuki was inspired by a real Meiji-era samurai: Kawakami Gensai, one of the four most feared hitokiri of the period.
"Initial D" by Shuichi Shigeno made the Toyota AE86 famous: after the manga, used car prices skyrocketed among Japanese collectors.
Minoru Shiraishi, voice of Tanaka in "Lucky Star", actually sang live during recordings: his improvisations went directly into the episodes.
"Yu-Gi-Oh!" started as a horror manga in 1996: card games only appeared later and became the series' focus at the publisher's request.
Director Mamoru Hosoda was rejected by Studio Ghibli as director of "Howl's Moving Castle" and turned that experience into the courage to found Studio Chizu.
"Inuyasha" by Rumiko Takahashi ran for twelve years from 1996 to 2008: the manga spans 558 chapters set between modern and feudal Japan.
"Hajime no Ippo" by George Morikawa has been running since 1989 with over 140 volumes: it's one of the longest-running sports manga in history.
Koichi Yamadera voiced Spike in "Cowboy Bebop" and the Genie in the Japanese "Aladdin": he's considered the most vocally versatile seiyuu in Japan.
"Digimon Adventure" launched in 1999 as a Pokémon rival but developed more mature storylines: fans consider it superior in long-term storytelling.
Studio Shaft is known for its exaggerated "head tilts" in "Monogatari": the impossible head angles became both a meme and a visual trademark.
"Trigun" by Yasuhiro Nightow was published in different magazines due to editorial issues: the manga changed publishers mid-story, a rare case in the industry.
Aya Hirano, voice of Haruhi Suzumiya, actually sang "God Knows" live: the concert scene in the anime went viral well before the YouTube era.
"Escaflowne" blended fantasy, mecha, and shōjo in 1996: Yoko Kanno composed the soundtrack with Gregorian choirs, making it unique in the anime landscape.
Toshio Suzuki, Studio Ghibli's producer, convinced Miyazaki to make "Princess Mononoke" by showing him the moss-covered forests of Yakushima.
"Shingeki no Kyojin" was rejected by Shūeisha before being accepted by Kōdansha: Jump editors deemed the artwork too rough.
Akio Ōtsuka, voice of Batou in "Ghost in the Shell", is the son of Chikao Ōtsuka, voice of Golgo 13: father and son voiced iconic characters for decades.
"Tengen Toppa Gurren Lagann" was the first major production by Studio Trigger's future team, made under the Gainax label in 2007.
The manga "Vagabond" by Takehiko Inoue has been on hiatus since 2015: its ink and watercolor pages require production time incompatible with serialization.
"Lupin III: The Woman Called Fujiko Mine" (2012) was the first series in the franchise directed by a woman, Sayo Yamamoto, with a radically different visual style.
"Toradora!" popularized the term "tsundere" in global anime vocabulary: Taiga Aisaka became the definitive archetype of the character trait.
Studio Ghibli temporarily shut down its production department in 2014 after Miyazaki's retirement: it reopened when the director decided to return for one last film.
"Great Pretender" by WIT Studio was one of the first anime produced specifically for Netflix, with international settings and Freddie Mercury music in the credits.
Romi Park voiced Edward Elric in "Fullmetal Alchemist" and Hange Zoë in "Attack on Titan": she's one of the most versatile seiyuu, known for both male and female roles.
"Dorohedoro" by Q Hayashida was serialized for 18 years across three different magazines: the mangaka's grotesque, chaotic style made her a cult author.
"Crayon Shin-chan" lost its creator Yoshito Usui in 2009 in a mountain accident: the manga was continued by his team of assistants.
The first Italian edition of "Dragon Ball" was published by Star Comics in 1995 with a flipped format for Western reading: fans only discovered the original direction later.
"Kaiji" by Nobuyuki Fukumoto uses a sharp, unconventional art style: despite its atypical look, it's one of the most critically acclaimed psychological manga.
In Japan, the word "anime" refers to any animated film, including Disney or Pixar: the distinction between anime and cartoons is a Western invention.
"Tokyo Ghoul" by Sui Ishida was drawn entirely digitally on a graphics tablet: the author completed both the original manga and the sequel ":re" in six years.
Junichi Suwabe, voice of Sukuna in "Jujutsu Kaisen" and Archer in "Fate", also narrates nature documentaries for Japanese television.
"Fate/stay night" began as a visual novel in 2004: the franchise spawned anime, films, manga, and games, becoming one of Japan's most profitable IPs.
Mari Okada, screenwriter of "Anohana" and "Maquia", revealed in her autobiography that she was a hikikomori as a teenager before entering the anime industry.
"Slam Dunk" ended abruptly in 1996 by Inoue's own decision: the publisher wanted to continue, but the author considered the story complete after the national tournament.
"Ping Pong the Animation" by Masaaki Yuasa used a deliberately rough, distorted art style: critics considered it one of the best sports anime ever made.
Miyazaki hand-drew every single storyboard for his films: his e-konte are so detailed they've been published as standalone volumes.
"Black Lagoon" by Rei Hiroe is set in Thailand with criminal protagonists: the manga has been on frequent hiatus since the 2010s due to the author's work pace.
The Italian dub of "Naruto" cast Leonardo Graziano as the protagonist, who followed the character from childhood through "Boruto" for nearly twenty years.
"K-On!" by Kyoto Animation in 2009 caused a boom in guitar and bass sales in Japan: thousands of girls started playing instruments inspired by the series.
Junji Ito, master of horror manga, draws his disturbing stories in a bright, tidy studio: in private life he's described as a cheerful and kind person.
"Summer Time Rendering" was published on the digital platform Shōnen Jump+, proving that online manga could compete with traditional print magazines.
Comiket has an unwritten rule: professional mangaka participate as amateur creators, selling dōjinshi of their own characters alongside fans.
"Suzume" by Makoto Shinkai in 2022 became the second Japanese film to surpass $200 million worldwide at the box office, after "Your Name" by the same director.
Studio Production I.G produced both "Ghost in the Shell" and the animated sequence in "Kill Bill Vol. 1" at Quentin Tarantino's direct request.
"My Neighbor Totoro" was a box office disappointment in 1988: it only became a cultural phenomenon through merchandise and TV reruns in the following years.
Hideaki Anno and Hayao Miyazaki have a complex relationship: Anno voiced the lead in "The Wind Rises" (2013), chosen by Miyazaki for his non-actor voice.
"Baki" by Keisuke Itagaki has been running since 1991 with over 150 volumes across its series: the martial arts manga has never stopped for over thirty years.
"Violet Evergarden" by Kyoto Animation was one of the first anime produced after the 2019 arson attack: the 2020 film was dedicated to the victims of the tragedy.
Mamoru Miyano, voice of Light Yagami in "Death Note" and Dabi in "My Hero Academia", is also a singer with published albums and sold-out concerts in Japan.
"The Cat Returns" by Studio Ghibli originated as a spin-off of "Whisper of the Heart": the Baron was a minor character in the earlier film.
In Japan, there's an Evangelion-themed train on the Hakone line: the cars reproduce the Eva units' colors and stations feature character announcements.
